newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders drop in November.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders drop in November.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods dropped unexpectedly in November because of weaker demand for computer components and communications equipment, the Commerce Department said Friday.

New orders for all types of durable goods fell 1.6 percent in November to a seasonally adjusted $171.8 billion -- the first decline in three months and in sharp contrast to Wall Street economists' expectations for a 0.1 percent rise in orders.

The decrease in November orders followed a revised 0.5 percent increase in October and a 4.5 percent rise in September orders. Previously, the department said October orders had risen only 0.3 percent.
The last time that durable goods orders fell before last month was in August, when they were down 3.6 percent.
Though November orders declined, shipments of finished goods were up 0.8 percent to $170.1 billion after falling 1.2 percent in October.
The department said key factors accounting for the pickup in shipments last month included a strong gain in electronic and electrical equipment and more shipments of commercial aircraft and parts.
New orders for transportation equipment were flat in November at $41.6 billion following a 6.8 percent drop in October.
Transportation equipment accounts for about one-quarter of total durable goods, so shifts in demand can affect the monthly report strongly.

Excluding transportation, Commerce said orders in November plummeted 2.2 percent -- the biggest monthly decline in nearly four years since a 2.4 percent drop in January 1993 -- following a 3 percent jump in October.

Orders for durable goods, items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years, are an indicator of the manufacturing sector's vigour, which in turn weighs heavily on the overall economy.

New orders for electronic and electrical equipment plunged 9.3 percent last month to $28.2 billion after a 16.9 percent jump in October. Department officials said orders fell for computer components including circuit boards, semiconductors and transistors.
Orders for defence goods, which experience wide monthly swings, shot up by 55.2 percent to $8.3 billion after a 2 percent rise in October.
If defence is excluded, overall durable goods orders in November were down 3.4 percent after rising 0.4 percent in October.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, fell 7.8 percent last month to $43.6 billion after declining 0.4 percent in October.
Unfilled orders increased in November by 0.3 percent to $488.5 billion following a 1.2 percent October rise -- the sixth gain in seven months.

Orders for industrial machinery were up 0.3 percent in November to $31.9 billion after a 1.7 percent decrease in October. Primary metals orders gained 0.2 percent to $14.4 billion after a 1.9 percent October decline.
